nodes.title: Detailed in-plant cooling-water process representation within coupled water-power operation
nodes.hypothesis_to_test: Within the five-paper pilot, clear prose describing in-plant cooling-water demand/process as part of a study's own model is less common than generic water-power dependence; author-identified future work may point to remaining modeling opportunities.
nodes.interpretation: The pilot evidence supports further testing of this candidate direction, not a field-wide claim. No conclusion is made about equation types, detailed thermodynamic fidelity, or prevalence beyond these five papers.

nodes.title: Fast information-layer sensing integrated with slower water/thermal dynamics for early warning or closed-loop control
nodes.hypothesis_to_test: Explicit prose linking fast cyber/information sensing to slower physical dynamics and to early warning/active control is uncommon in the pilot corpus, even where multistage or anticipatory operation appears.
nodes.interpretation: The pilot supports keeping 4-1 as a candidate hypothesis and clarifies the construct boundary; it does not verify field-wide absence.

nodes.title: Extending infrastructure service-loss analysis to critical facilities, populations, and social vulnerability
nodes.hypothesis_to_test: The pilot corpus often stops at network performance or facility/region description rather than quantifying population exposure or social vulnerability across the impact chain.
nodes.interpretation: The pilot gives a plausible, limited basis to test 5-1 in a wider corpus; it is not a confirmatory field-level gap.

nodes.title: 3.1. Test system
nodes.text: A grid-connected MG integrating a WSS is used to verify the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. The renewable generation, electric loads, hydraulic loads and electricity price are shown in Fig. 5 [30]. Fig. 6 shows the typical WSS [10]. Without loss of generality, the large WSS can be split three sub-systems marked as ①②③. The rated desalination power is set to 600 kW, and the water supply parameters are shown in Table 1 in appendix [23]. Considering the natural precipitation, the daily freshwater production is set to 2100 m3 in summer and 3150 m3 in winter, respectively. To show the superiority of the proposed strategy, three cases are compared, as follows: Case 1: The novel WSS model is used to carry out demand side response using the proposed dispatching strategy. Case 2: The WSS is dispatched to respond to the MG demand according to [23], where the WSS cannot be split and the DD always works at rated power. Case 3: The WSS carries out demand side response according to electricity price [22], where the WSS cannot be split and the DD works at rated power. The simulations are coded in MATLAB and solved by Gurobi on a Windows-based PC with 8 GB of RAM.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-01-ZD-S14-4-C001
nodes.title: 4. Conclusion
nodes.text: This paper proposes an optimal energy management strategy for a Fig. 17. Real-time electric and hydraulic balance in case 3. renewable MG integrating WSSs. A novel water supply model is presented that considers the large system split feasibility, hydraulic stability, and desalination characteristic. To ensure the performance of the MG integrating WSSs, a two-stage scheduling method is designed for minimizing the MG operational costs and power fluctuations. This scheduling problem is efficiently solved by a two-stage algorithm. The simulation study indicates that the energy-water management strategy can carry out energy arbitrage, power smoothing while supporting the external grid simultaneously. The novel water supply model can significantly improve the operational flexibility of the DD and WP. The desalination loss and water distribution loss can be reduced by more than 7.1% and 5.2%, respectively. Additionally, using the proposed scheduling strategy, the operational cost of the MG integrating WSSs can be reduced by 19.5%. The hydraulic and electric stability can also be ensured. However, some technical details neglected in the theoretical discussion of this paper may be of great importance in practical application. Therefore, we will conduct a real case study in the future. Additionally, the extreme weather significantly affects the reliability of the power supply. The resilience of power gird integrating water supply systems will also our future work.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-02-ZA-ABSTRACT-C001
nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.text: This paper proposes a model for optimizing the energy ﬂexibility of water distribution systems (WDSs) in dayahead power systems operation. The water distribution system operators (W-DSOs) are considered as energy-conscious entities, who run the proposed WDS operation model to optimize the operation of pumps and tanks for minimizing the operation cost of local WDSs, given the expected water demand and electricity prices of the next day. A WDS energy ﬂexibility model is proposed that is used by W-DSOs in order to calculate and offer the feasible ﬂexible energy capacity to the power system operator. The proposed WDS operation model takes into account the hydraulic operating constraints of water networks, thus ensuring deliverability of the WDS energy ﬂexibility. Further, a network-constrained unit commitment model is proposed that integrates and optimizes the energy ﬂexibility of WDSs in the day-ahead operation of power systems. The proposed model is implemented on a 15-node WDS that is powered by a 6-bus power system and the results are presented to study the impacts of optimized WDS energy ﬂexibility on power and water systems operation.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-03-ZB-S07-3-1-C002
nodes.title: 3.1. Infrastructure System Resilience Deﬁnition
nodes.text: Therefore, infrastructure system resilience includes two basic concepts: System performance and its adaptive capacity. The system resilience can be divided into two diﬀerent forms: Proactive absorptive capacity and reactive restorative capacity. Proactive absorptive capacity mainly depends on the infrastructure (or network) inherent features, such as robustness, which can be determined in the infrastructure planning and design, or disaster preparation and mitigation period. Reactive restorative capacity mainly depends on the restorative strategies implemented during the operation period after the disturbance. This kind of classiﬁcation is more practical for resilience improvement. Since the number of functioning infrastructure elements and the number of available resources are the foundations for recovery, the former capacity will directly inﬂuence the latter. In Equation (6), the adaptive capacity is deﬁned using dynamic system performance, which is similar to the quality function of the resilience model derived by MCEER (Multidisciplinary Center for Earthquake Engineering Research) [30]. System performance curve includes the capacity to withstand and recover (see Figure 5).

It could be [km] of unblocked street length, [km3] of water distribution volume, [kw] of power transmission capacity and [GB] of Internet traﬃc information volume. According to Figure 5, infrastructure systems may have the same performance and the same resilience, but one could be due to high robustness and low rapidity, while the other could be due to low robustness and high rapidity [48]. The former is reactive, absorptive capacity; the latter is proactive restorative capacity. Infrastructure system, a typical “systems of systems”, is a set of multiple and independently operational systems (such as street network, water supply network and power supply network, etc.) interacting with one another to meet speciﬁc needs [49]. Therefore, infrastructure system resilience refers not only to the ability to resist disturbance and reorganize intra-layer network layers, while undergoing change, but also the ability to retain essentially the same function, structure and feedbacks among inter-layer networks.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-03-ZB-S21-5-2-C001
nodes.title: 5.2. Infrastructures Interdependence Formulation for the Test Case Study
nodes.section_title: 5.2. Infrastructures Interdependence Formulation for the Test Case Study
nodes.text: This research and the test developed for evaluating a proposed resilience measure include ﬁve basic dependence patterns, always present among diverse infrastructure types. (i) Street-water supply network: Nodes of street and water supply networks located in the same geographic area, which means geographical dependence and use of Equation (5). (ii) Street-power grid: Nodes of street and power supply networks located in the same geographic area have geographical dependence and use of Equation (5). Power plants need fuel (such as coal) from outside, which means node-path dependence pattern and use of Equation (4). (iii) Water supply-power grid: Water supply facilities, including waterworks, storage facilities and pump stations are powered by the eclectic infrastructure located in the same geographic area, which means node-node dependence and use of Equation (1). Power plants are provided with water by the water supply facilities in the same geographic area, which means node-edge dependence and use of Equation (2). (iv) Street-information infrastructure network: Nodes of street and infrastructure networks are located in the same geographic area, which means geographical dependence and use of Equation (5). (v) Power grid-information infrastructure network: Every electric transmission control depends on the information infrastructure (SCADA systems and similar), which refers to node-node dependence and use of Equation (1).

nodes.label: B001-PDF-03-ZC-S23-5-4-C001
nodes.title: 5.4. Simulation of Test Network System Performance
nodes.section_title: 5.4. Simulation of Test Network System Performance
nodes.text: Sustainability 2019, 11, 6552 20 of 31 node-cluster dependence and use of Equation (3). Information control center and Internet service providers are powered by the electric infrastructure located in the same geographic area, which refers to the node-node or node-edge dependencies and use of Equation (1) or (2). (vi) Water supply-information infrastructure network: Nodes of water supply and information networks are located in the same geographic area, which means geographical dependence and use of Equation (5). In the test example, elements, including nodes and edges in a network, have the same importance, which means that the service level of the same type of infrastructure is the same. The buﬀering time TB and the repair time TR for every infrastructure are assumed to be one day. Though diﬀerent sectors have diﬀerent types of resources, it is assumed that one unit of resources have the same eﬀectiveness in repairing one infrastructure system component. For simpliﬁcation, every sector is assumed to have two units of resources that can be used at the beginning. In the network theory, disturbance to the infrastructure system is always represented as the removal of nodes and/or edges from the infrastructure system network.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-03-ZD-S31-7-C002
nodes.title: 7. Conclusions
nodes.text: This model is not only a framework for system-of-systems resilience analysis, but also provides an evaluation method of various protection and restoration strategies that will optimize the performance of interdependent infrastructure system. With a numerical test, the simulation results show that the sector-speciﬁc decisions could not always lead to optimal system solutions, i.e., infrastructure systems with RS-IE always end with the lowest resilience. In the paper, the amount and eﬀectiveness of resources are assumed the same among diﬀerent sectors. This limits the results of the analyses and points out that restoration resources should not be evenly distributed, but based on the sector’s contribution to system-level resilience improvement. Therefore, the resilience model can also be used for planning and distribution of restoration resources. This paper simpliﬁes the real infrastructure system structure and uses a numerical test for illustrative purposes. However, it is very clear that the framework can be easily extended to evaluate system resilience under other types of disasters. Social, economic and organizational resilience can also be analyzed with the community and organization management data provided. Thus, the framework can be used by the municipal decision makers for a community resilience improvement under various types of disasters by development and timely preparation of disaster management emergency plans.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-03-ZD-S31-7-C003
nodes.title: 7. Conclusions
nodes.text: Finally, actual infrastructure systems are of high complexity. Proactive absorptive capacity and reactive restorative capacity interact through changing robustness and resourcefulness of the infrastructure system. The numerical test presented in the paper only takes the latter into account. In addition, this paper only considers cascading failures caused by the near physical failure of elements. Addressing the malfunctions generated by the ﬂow overload along the path and analyzing their impacts on system restoration processes and resilience are topics for further research. The future research will also focus on the interaction of the reactive absorptive capacity and proactive restorative capacity in a real case study. nodes.label: B001-PDF-04-ZA-S01-I-C001
nodes.title: I. INTRODUCTION
nodes.text: system (WDS) are two operationally interdependent criti-cal infrastructure systems that have been recognized and studied in broad generalities for some time. The main dependence of the EPS on the WDS is the water required for the cooling cycle of thermoelectric power generation. The main dependence of the WDS on the EPS is the electric power needed for pumping water from a source to the treatment plant and end-user through the WDS. The interdependencies become critical under conditions oflimitedwaterand/orelectricityavailability.Theoptimization– simulation framework [1] used for this article accounts for these interdependencies. If power plant cooling water demands are not met, then the EPS may fail to supply adequate electric power for WDS pumping stations leading to a cascading failure of both systems. This article presents new metrics and a new methodology for computation of infrastructural–operational resilience (IOR) for real-time operations of WDS and EPS under critical conditions of limited water and/or limited electrical energy resulting from extreme drought or electric grid failure. IOR is calculated by weighting the operational resilience (OR) with the appropriate infrastructural resilience (IR) metrics.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-04-ZB-S04-II-C001
nodes.title: II. OPTIMIZATION–SIMULATION APPROACH
nodes.text: The IOR methodology was applied using the results from an optimization–simulation model application developed for extended time-period WDS–EPS operations [1]. The power system control optimization was implemented by a combination of unit commitment (UC) for determining the ON/OFF status of all the generators and a modiﬁed dc optimal power ﬂow (OPF) for determining generator output set-points. The power system network simulation for the operational time-frame simulations was accomplished by the use of time-series power ﬂows. The water system optimization–simulation was accomplished using an extended period simulation coupled with a genetic algorithm (GA) solution methodology for a control optimization model. The water system and the power system were interfaced by al-Fig. 2. Internet-worked simulation overview. network simulations via a program control overlay developed in python. Fig. 2 depicts an overview of this concept. The relevant simulation data exchanged between the power system and wa-ter network simulations included EPS network conﬁgurations, pump electric power consumption as an identiﬁable component of power system loads, and thermal generation cooling water requirements, which were used as node demands within the water system.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-04-ZC-S12-G-C001
nodes.title: G. EPS: Thermoelectric Generation Cooling Water
nodes.section_title: G. EPS: Thermoelectric Generation Cooling Water
nodes.text: Index Function Thermoelectric generation requires water for the cooling cy-cle in the process of converting the heated working ﬂuid from steam back to water via heat transfer. The closed-loop cooling cycle introduces losses through drift, blowdown, and evapora-tion. So, water is needed to “make-up” for the amount lost and represents a key dependence of the power system on the water system. Generation owners meet this need through external sources, such as a municipal water utility as well as by water that is stored onsite. Since the amount of onsite storage for cooling water is normally substantial [15], it is reasonable to assume that the levels of the water in the onsite tanks will not change vary rapidly. The index function relating system performance to the amount of cooling water that is being supplied is related to a conservative estimate of the storage tank level with a piecewise linear form as follows: ⟦PDF_GLYPH_U+000B⟧ ⟦PDF_GLYPH_U+000C⟧ TLg,t TLg,initial · 10 ceil Rg 10 . nodes.label: B001-PDF-04-ZC-S13-H-C001
nodes.title: H. EPS: Load Supplied (Overall) Index Function
nodes.section_title: H. EPS: Load Supplied (Overall) Index Function
nodes.text: The goal of power system operation is to satisfactorily supply the requested electrical power demands of consumers while sat-isfying constraints related to the quality of the power delivered. A resilience measure along these lines is formulated in order to quantify how well the system demands were met under extreme system operating conditions. Based on consumer surveys [31], consumers are willing to adjust their demands depending on the perceived weather conditions. These consumers are also observed to have different levels of willingness to change their consumption based on the knowledge of how the water and power systems interact as well as whether the curtailment of the usage of water and energy is mandatory or not. For representa-tion of this fact within this resilience calculation, the bus loads are decomposed into representative percentages for industrial, commercial, and residential components. Within the residential load component, it is further subdivided into single-family (sf) and multifamily (mf) elements based on recent census data for Arizona [32]. An example of how incorporation of this consumer data will affect the load curve over time is demonstrated below.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-04-ZC-S15-IV-C001
nodes.title: IV. COMPUTATION OF OPERATIONAL RESILIENCE
nodes.text: The deﬁnition for OR for an engineered system for each index function f in the WDS and EPS at time t is calculated as Resf,t = # of times satisfactory follows unsatisfactory # of times unsatisfactory occurs . (11) This article uses this deﬁnition of OR for deriving the equa-tions for OR under emergency conditions. Unsatisfactory op-eration is deﬁned as the resilience index function value being less than that function’s value in the previous simulation hour (and satisfactory operation denoted by an increase in the index function’s value). The measure of performance is deﬁned for real values between 0 and 1.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-04-ZC-S29-C-C001
nodes.title: C. WDS: Demand Priority Metric
nodes.text: Demand priority is an important robustness parameter during extreme water shortage and limited electric power availability conditions. A demand pattern is deﬁned for each service area in a WDS. The demand priority metric is simply a priority weight given to each service area z to ensure robustness with respect to demand satisfaction at higher priority service areas. The demand priority metric (Mdemand,z) values are assigned a noninteger value between 0 and 1 for each service area in the system depending on the type of demands (residential, commercial, industrial, or cooling water for power plants) in the service area.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-04-ZD-S47-A-C001
nodes.title: A. Example EPS
nodes.text: The example power system was a modiﬁed version of the IEEE 14 bus system [35], which is shown in Fig. 5. The mod-iﬁcations included the addition of representative distribution systems [36] to which the water system pumping station loads were mapped. Data for the distribution systems were generated fromtheIEEE34-bustestdistributionsystem[37].Theapproach taken here is equivalent to modeling the voltages for voltage lev-els at and above the subtransmission system for all of the system, except where the critical interdependencies of the power system with the water system lie. Fig. 5 shows how the one-line-diagram of the 14-bus system and the two additional distribution systems were mapped spatially to the water system and vice versa. In order to create time varying system loads, historical load data [38] were normalized and used as LMF within the test system. The short-term security constrained UC for each hour was run every 24 h during the simulation using the next 24 LMF’s, which had their indices offset according to the current time period in the simulation. Fig. 6 shows the LMF pattern that was used for the power system.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-04-ZD-S48-B-C001
nodes.title: B. Example WDS
nodes.text: The example water system is a hypothetical WDS modeling demands from two cities and the power system described above. Fig. 6. LMF for one-month simulation. Cooling water is supplied to the power plants in the WDS from both a freshwater source and a reclaimed water source (shown in Fig. 5). This cooling water is pumped to each power plant through a freshwater pumping station and a reclaimed water pumping station. The WDS control optimization–simulation model attempts to maximize the supply of reclaimed water for power plants. City 1 has four service areas with a total base demand of 30 000 gpm. City 2 has ﬁve service areas with a total base demand of 25000 gpm. A total of 17 freshwater pumps (WP) and 11 reclaimed water pumps (RWP) serve the overall WDS. Cooling water demands for power plants, on an hourly Fig. 7. Trends of water availability. basis, are input to the WDS optimization–simulation model from the EPS optimization–simulation model. Each power plant in the system is equipped with onsite water storage equivalent to a two-week average water consumption.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-04-ZD-S52-X-C002
nodes.title: X. CONCLUSION
nodes.text: In addition, the IOR methodology could be applied to forecasted, extreme, megadrought scenarios for more accurate system simulations and anticipatory policy making. The IOR computation methodology presented in this article does not consider component failures in either system in the computation procedure. Because the resilience calculations for the test systems shown are not computationally expensive (total calculation time of 1.37s for EPS + 1.90s for WDS = 3.27s total), it seems that the IOR computation methodology could be used for both postsimulation as well as real-time EPS–WDS perfor-mance assessment. Therefore, future work will involve applica-tion of the developed IOR computation methodology to larger WDS and EPS test systems. The scalability of the proposed metrics is currently being investigated for larger test systems and will be incorporated in future research. Moving the ap-plication toward larger, more realistic test systems also war-rants the inclusions of a developed middleware architecture, which emulates the supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) communication that would be necessary for data exchange between the two networks.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-05-ZC-S10-2-4-C001
nodes.title: 2.4. Seismic performance analysis for the PWS based on the energy
nodes.section_title: 2.4. Seismic performance analysis for the PWS based on the energy
nodes.text: failure model This study focuses on the short-term seismic performance assessment of PWS specifically at the urban scale. Consequently, this study strictly concentrates on the unidirectional power-to-water dependency. Under earthquake hazards, PSs not only experience power reduction but also cause functional degradation of associated WDS components, potentially resulting in localized or widespread water supply shortages for end-users. Based on reconnaissance reports from the Los Angeles earthquake [20] and Wenchuan earthquake [21], it can be seen that the functional state of the PWS under seismic hazards is better represented by a continuous model than a binary model, which is shown in Fig. 4. To describe this continuous mapping state of the PWS after an earthquake, this study proposes an energy-dependent failure model. Eq. (10) denotes the actual active power that the i th substation can supply to its dependent water treatment plant after the earthquake, which incorporates parameters of post-earthquake power supply at the substation and the backup power supply to the water treatment plant. Eq. (11) further describes the relationship between backup power availability to the water treatment plant. Eq. (12) represents the ratio of postto pre-earthquake power of the i th substation.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-05-ZC-S15-3-4-C003
nodes.title: 3.4. Influence of backup power facility in water pump station
nodes.section_title: 3.4. Influence of backup power facility in water pump station
nodes.text: However, under higher earthquake magnitude scenarios, both P(W|E) and α exert significant controlling effects on the system performance. Therefore, implementation measures—such as elevating the power supply priority for WTPs (i.e., assigning a smaller α), and ensuring the reliability of backup generators—can effectively boost the seismic performance of the PWS. Specifically, Fig. 16(b) demonstrates that increasing the backup power availability P(W|E) from 0% to 54% yields the same performance improvement as lowering α from 0.7 to 0.3. Thus, in practical disaster mitigation scenarios where high backup power availability cannot be strictly guaranteed, prioritizing power allocation to WTPs (elevating their supply priority) serves as a highly effective alternative strategy to mitigate the seismic cascading risk of urban PWS.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-05-ZD-S11-3-C001
nodes.title: 3. Case study
nodes.text: This section first introduces the power-water system (PWS) case in Shelby County, Tennessee. Subsequently, the analysis of different dependent failure models and the evolution of seismic performance under varying earthquake intensities are performed to verify the effectiveness of the energy-dependent failure model. Furthermore, the evolution comparison between the Shelby case and the NY case is carried out to reveal how the topological and functional characteristics of PWS influence the seismic performance. Finally, a dependent parameter sensitivity analysis on the seismic performance of PWS is performed to identify critical links and parameters that affect cascading failures in PWS. The case study of the PWS in Shelby is employed to analyze the seismic performance of PWS using different dependent failure models [42]. As shown in Fig. 6, the water distribution system (WDS) of this PWS comprises 9 water sources, 71 pipelines, and 49 user nodes, whereas its power system (PS) consists of 8 power plants, 21 12-kV substations, 30 23-kV substations, and 71 distribution lines. This study selects the New Madrid Seismic Zone (NMSZ), situated northwest of Shelby County, with an earthquake magnitude of MW=7.5 and a hypocenter depth of 10 km [43].

nodes.label: B001-PDF-05-ZD-S17-4-C001
nodes.title: 4. Conclusions
nodes.text: To investigate the seismic performance of dependent power-water systems (PWS) during earthquake hazards, this study proposes an energy-dependent failure model for the power system (PS) and water distribution system (WDS) based on the power flow models and hydraulic models. This dependent failure model characterizes the cascading failure propagation process between these two heterogeneous infrastructure systems through energy conservation based on the dependent substations and pumps of the water treatment plant. The characteristic analyses on PWS cases are conducted with varying earthquake magnitudes, topologies, and functional characteristics. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: (i) The fundamental assumptions of dependency failure models critically dictate the seismic performance outcomes of the PWS, with variations reaching up to 90.9%. The binary-dependent model may overestimate seismic performance losses, and different thresholds led to WDS seismic performance variation ranging from 19.3% to 90.9%. In contrast, the energy-dependent failure model proposed by this study can continuously characterize the impact of partial functional failures in substations on WTP functionality, without relying on threshold parameters. (ii) The difference in the seismic performance of PWSs evaluated by the binary-dependent model and the energy-dependent model decreases as the magnitude increases.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-05-ZD-S17-4-C003
nodes.title: 4. Conclusions
nodes.text: Specially, in disaster scenarios where WTP backup power supplies are unavailable or fail to operate, proactively prioritizing grid power assignment to WTPs (i.e., assign power supply to WTPs by residual power capacity in substations) serves as a highly effective emergency response strategy to maximize the seismic performance of WDS. Overall, this study concentrates on the seismic performance assessment within the PWS, aiming to reveal the energy transfer amid power system-water system-users with a unidirectional dependency between substations and water treatment plants. However, the PS and the WDS exhibit complex interdependencies, and there are still several limitations in this study: (i) The proposed energy-dependent model characterizes the degradation of power transmission from substations to WTPs under seismic hazards through energy conservation among active power, water head, and flow rate. However, the reverse dependency of the PS on the WDS is not addressed. Quantifying the energy dependence of power plants or substation cooling systems on water supply capacity will be a critical focus for future research. (ii) This study conducts a steady-state power flow analysis tailored to city-scale distribution networks in evaluating the seismic performance of the PS.

nodes.label: B001-PDF-05-ZD-S17-4-C004
nodes.title: 4. Conclusions
nodes.text: However, expanding the spatial scope to a regional scale to incorporate the seismic vulnerability of transmission networks and adopting a detailed power flow model to capture more failure mechanisms present a significant challenge and a crucial direction for future work. (iii) Regarding the facility damage to the WDS, this study primarily accounts for pipeline damage and the loss of power supply to WTPs. Incorporating the direct structural damage to WTPs into the proposed framework, and evaluating how such physical damage degrades the overall functionality of the broader PWS, will be another key priority in subsequent studies.
